concepts.title: The search range and the midpoint
concepts.summary: Binary search finds a target in a sorted list by keeping a range lo..hi that always holds the target and checking the middle element.

keyPoints.statement: Binary search only works when the list is sorted.

evidence.quote: Binary search only works when the list is sorted.

keyPoints.statement: The invariant: the target, if present, is always inside the range from lo to hi.

evidence.quote: The target, if it is present, is always inside the range from lo to hi.

keyPoints.statement: mid = (lo + hi) // 2: integer division rounds down, so the midpoint is the left middle element of an even range.

evidence.quote: Integer division rounds down, so when the range has an even number of elements the midpoint is the left one of the two middle elements.

keyPoints.statement: If the middle element is smaller than the target, the search continues in the right half.

evidence.quote: If the middle element is smaller than the target, the target can only be to the right, so the search continues in the right half.

keyPoints.statement: Binary search returns the index of the target, not the target itself.

evidence.quote: Binary search returns the index of the target, not the target itself.

keyPoints.statement: When the target is not in the list, this version returns -1.

evidence.quote: When the target is not in the list, this version returns -1.

concepts.title: Loop bounds and off-by-one errors
concepts.summary: Most binary search bugs are off-by-one errors in the loop condition and the range updates.
prerequisites: The search range and the midpoint

keyPoints.statement: The loop condition is lo <= hi.

evidence.quote: The loop condition is lo <= hi.

keyPoints.statement: A loop that uses lo < hi stops one step too early and can miss a target in the last remaining position.

evidence.quote: A loop that uses lo < hi stops one step too early and can miss a target that sits in the last remaining position.

keyPoints.statement: The updates must exclude the middle element: lo = mid + 1 and hi = mid - 1.

evidence.quote: The updates must exclude the middle element, because it has already been checked.

keyPoints.statement: Writing lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1 can cause an infinite loop.

evidence.quote: Writing lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1 can cause an infinite loop

keyPoints.statement: The loop ends when lo becomes greater than hi: the range is empty and the target is not in the list.

evidence.quote: the loop ends when lo becomes greater than hi, which means the range is empty and the target is not in the list

keyPoints.statement: The safe midpoint mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2 gives the same result without the large sum.

evidence.quote: The safe form is mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2, which gives the same result without the large sum.

concepts.title: Running time
concepts.summary: Halving the range every step makes binary search O(log n); the price is that the list must be sorted.
prerequisites: The search range and the midpoint

keyPoints.statement: Because the range is halved at every step, binary search runs in O(log n) time.

evidence.quote: Because the range is halved at every step, the number of steps grows with the logarithm of the list size, so binary search runs in O(log n) time.

keyPoints.statement: The worst case is floor(log2(n)) + 1 comparisons.

evidence.quote: In the worst case, binary search on a list of n elements makes floor(log2(n)) + 1 comparisons of the middle element.

keyPoints.statement: Doubling the size of the list adds only one more step in the worst case.

evidence.quote: Doubling the size of the list adds only one more step in the worst case.

keyPoints.statement: Linear search runs in O(n) time.

evidence.quote: Linear search checks the elements one by one and runs in O(n) time.

keyPoints.statement: The best case for binary search is 1 comparison.

evidence.quote: The best case for binary search is 1 comparison, when the target is the first middle element.

keyPoints.statement: The list must be sorted first, which takes O(n log n) time, so one search on an unsorted list is better done linearly.

evidence.quote: The speed has a price: the list must be sorted first, and sorting takes O(n log n) time.
